title: ⚙️ Technology, Craft & Infrastructure
rawNotionMarkup: Eryndor's everyday technological foundation is broadly high-medieval fantasy, with pockets of mechanical sophistication and a distinctive steam-and-engineering influence. Technology develops unevenly between regions and civilisations. The Khazari are among the world's most mechanically and metallurgically advanced peoples, but they do not represent the technological level of every kingdom. ## Overall technological character Eryndor combines: - High-medieval daily life: castles, walled towns, roads, swords, axes, bows, crossbows, siege engines, smithies, mills, guilds, traditional craftsmanship and horse-drawn transport. - Advanced regional engineering: mechanical pumps, ventilation, industrial machinery, sophisticated foundries, hydraulic systems, runic regulators and specialist mining equipment. - Rare or experimental devices: steam-powered land engines, gyrocopters, airships and unusual magical transport. The setting may have steampunk flavour, especially in Khazari industrial and mining contexts, without becoming a modern or fully Victorian industrial world. ## Khazari engineering and industry Khazari engineering is highly developed, particularly in mining, metallurgy, machinery, stonework and rune-integrated systems. Established or accepted Khazari technologies include: - Steam-powered mining equipment. - Mechanical pumps and drainage systems. - Mechanical ventilation for underground works. - Industrial rail carts within mining and industrial complexes. - Advanced foundries and metalworking facilities. - Hydraulic systems and heavy engineering. - Runic machinery and regulators integrated with mechanical systems. - Artillery, siege machinery and armoured land engines. - Gyrocopters, which are rare, expensive and not ordinary everyday transport. Khazari underground infrastructure can include steam-driven lifts, mechanical machinery, reinforced galleries, pumps, ventilation systems and runic controls. These technologies should feel like the result of generations of craft knowledge, skilled labour and local investment—not mass-produced modern devices. The Seven Mountain Thrones are culturally and politically distinct. Their industries, resources, engineering schools and access to advanced devices may differ. ## Everyday technologies and material life Across Eryndor, people use familiar pre-industrial and high-medieval tools and infrastructure: - Hand tools, anvils, bellows, furnaces, forges and water-powered mills. - Horse-drawn carts, wagons and passenger coaches. - Sailing vessels and established maritime craft. - Roads, bridges, ports, fortifications, gates and caravan routes. - Bows, crossbows, swords, axes, spears, shields and mechanical siege weapons. - Traditional masonry, carpentry, textiles, leatherwork, pottery, glasswork and metalcraft. - Waterwheels, windmills, pumps, drainage works and local public infrastructure. Not every town has the same access to technology. Wealth, geography, trade, skilled workers, guilds, political stability and local resources determine what is available. ## Transport and travel technologies Established transport forms include: - Walking, riding horses, pack animals and animal-drawn wagons. - Passenger coaches and merchant caravans. - Sailing ships and other regionally appropriate vessels. - The Khazari Deepways, an extensive engineered underground road network. - Industrial rail carts in mining and industrial complexes. - Experimental steam-powered mechanical land engines. - Gyrocopters and airships, where available and appropriate. - Some forms of magical transport. - Rare dragon riding. Availability, cost, range, speed, reliability and legal access vary. Gyrocopters and airships are not common public transport for ordinary people. Dragon riding is exceptionally rare and should not be treated as a routine travel service. ### Deepways The Deepways are established Khazari underground highways connecting the Seven Mountain Thrones and linking mines, fortress-gates, subterranean settlements, engineering stations and trade depots. Their construction, uses, limitations and hazards are documented on the World Foundations & Geography page. They are not one perfectly mapped or universally open tunnel. ## Steam and mechanical systems Steam technology is present in some Khazari industrial and mining contexts. Mechanical pumps, ventilation, lifts, rail carts and specialist equipment are established. Some experimental steam-powered land engines also exist. These systems require: - Fuel and water. - Skilled operators and maintenance workers. - Reliable metalwork, seals, valves, boilers, gears and structural supports. - Replacement parts and access to workshops. - Safe ventilation and management of heat, pressure, smoke and exhaust. Steam machinery is not automatically compact, cheap, reliable or portable. Large machines may be noisy, heavy, expensive and maintenance-intensive. A mechanical device does not function without an infrastructure and workforce capable of operating it. ## Magic as a force shaping technological development Magic is not simply another tool layered on top of technology. It has helped shape which technologies Eryndor's societies needed to invent, which problems they chose to solve mechanically, and how far particular forms of engineering developed. In many parts of Eryndor, practical magic and enchanted craft can perform functions that, in our world, might eventually be addressed through electrical systems, chemical industry, automated machinery or modern communications. Modest heat, preservation, lighting, repair, detection, protection, signalling and other specialised workings can reduce the pressure to invent a mechanical or industrial equivalent. Where trained practitioners, prepared runes, enchanted components or magical services are available at a reasonable cost, a society may reasonably develop along a different path rather than reproduce the technological sequence of our own history. This is one important reason Eryndor does not simply progress toward modern technology. Its development is not a straight line from medieval machinery to electricity, electronics, cars and mass industrial automation. Magic changes the incentives, available solutions, infrastructure and economics. ### How magic and technology complement one another - Magic can substitute for some technologies: A warming rune may serve a purpose that would otherwise encourage mechanical heating; magical illumination may reduce the demand for certain lamp technologies; prepared charms or runic signals may provide specialised communication or detection without creating a modern electrical network. - Technology remains valuable where it is dependable or scalable: Pumps, ventilation, lifts, carts, ships, foundries, roads, gears and structural engineering solve practical problems through repeatable physical systems. They do not require every operator to be a trained mage. - Magitech combines both: Runic regulators, enchanted materials, binding frames and mechanically operated devices can support each other. Such systems still require skilled makers, materials, maintenance and careful design. - Magic is not free or unlimited: Practitioners, materials, preparation, training, access, reliability and local lunar conditions matter. A magical solution may be scarce, costly, specialised, regulated or unsuitable for continuous industrial use. - Technology can be preferable: A well-built pump or mechanical tool may be cheaper, more reliable and easier to maintain than a magical alternative. Not every task benefits from magic. - Local conditions determine the balance: Different regions and cultures may favour different combinations depending on resources, education, law, trade, tradition and the availability of magical practitioners. ### A different technological ceiling, not a frozen world Eryndor does have a technological boundary: the setting's general technological character remains high-medieval fantasy with sophisticated regional engineering and selected steam, hydraulic and magitech systems. It does not advance into a modern or fully Victorian industrial society. That boundary is not a ban on invention. Engineering, materials, machinery, craft methods, magical devices and infrastructure can improve within the established technological character. New developments should deepen or refine the world's existing paths rather than introduce an uncontrolled leap into modernity. Magic is part of the explanation for this different path, but it is not the only explanation. Geography, resources, institutions, labour, trade, political priorities, historical accidents and the uneven spread of knowledge also shape development. Do not claim that magic deliberately prevented invention everywhere, that all societies have equal access to it, or that a universal authority suppresses technology unless such facts are separately established. The result should feel like a world with its own mature balance of craft, machinery and magic—not a modern world with the names of technologies changed. ## Runic engineering and enchantment Khazari craft may integrate runes with mechanical systems. Runic regulators, enchantments and specialised components can support or stabilise machinery, but magic does not replace engineering principles. - A mechanical system still needs structural integrity, materials, maintenance and correct operation. - A rune's function depends on its design, arrangement, materials and the practitioner's skill. - A magical component may be difficult to manufacture, expensive to replace or dependent on a trained runesmith. - Ancient First Throne mechanisms may be far more sophisticated than modern systems, but their presence does not mean every modern machine is based on First Throne technology. - The current eastern mine's portable rune-binding frames and resonance equipment are specialist items, not proof of a general modern technology that can reproduce First Throne containment systems. ## Craft, metallurgy and specialist knowledge Craftsmanship is central to many Eryndoran societies. Khazari are especially renowned for metalworking, stonework, mining, engineering and rune-integrated manufacture. Metallurgy and craft should recognise the difference between: - Ore and refined metal. - Useful stock and flawed or contaminated material. - Smelting, refining, forging and heat treatment. - Iron, steel, alloys and their differing properties. - Structural defects, inclusions, grain, stress and fatigue. - The skill required to select, prepare, work and finish a material. The existence of advanced Khazari metallurgy does not mean every smith is a master or that high-quality material is cheap and plentiful. Skill, fuel, tools, time, access to ore and the quality of the workshop all matter. ## Uneven development across Eryndor Different peoples and regions develop technology according to their environments, resources, institutions, trade connections and history. - Khazari industrial and mining centres may have advanced steam systems and machinery. - Other regions may rely more heavily on water power, wind power, animal labour and traditional craft. - Merchant Republics may excel at shipbuilding, finance, navigation and commercial logistics. - Eldar craft may emphasise fine materials, precision and specialised enchanted work. - Urakai societies may develop engineering and military equipment suited to their plains, highlands and political structures. - Other cultures may have sophisticated technologies that are unfamiliar to Khazari observers. Do not assume a people is technologically backward because its inventions are different from Khazari machines. ## Technology boundaries The setting does not currently include: - Modern firearms or automatic weapons. - Electricity grids or electronic devices. - Cars or modern road networks. - Modern telecommunications or instant global communication. - Mass industrial production everywhere. - A fully Victorian industrial society. - Steam railways across the world as standard transport. The presence of steam engines, rail carts or advanced foundries does not imply modernity. Technology should remain grounded in the setting's materials, energy sources, labour, institutions and trade. ## Introducing a new invention New technology should have a plausible history and practical footprint. Establish, as appropriate: - Who invented or developed it, and where. - What problem it solves and why older methods were insufficient. - The materials, energy, tools and skilled labour it requires. - Its size, cost, reliability, risks and maintenance needs. - Who can afford it and who controls access. - How it affects trade, military power, labour, daily life and politics. - Whether it is experimental, specialist, regional, newly adopted or widespread. Do not introduce a major technological leap solely because it would be convenient for a scene. Inventions should spread gradually and unevenly, and their consequences should be believable.
